title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test — Mock Set D

passages.title: Passage 1
passages.instructions:
Questions 1–13

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on the reading passage below.
passages.body:
Deep freeze: the vault protecting the world's food supply

On a remote, ice-bound island roughly halfway between mainland Norway and the North Pole, a tunnel bores 130 metres into a mountainside. Behind a single steel door lie three chambers, each roughly the size of a swimming pool, holding row upon row of sealed boxes. Inside those boxes are seeds — millions of them, drawn from national and international collections in almost every country on Earth. This is the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, sometimes nicknamed the 'Doomsday Vault', and its sole purpose is to make sure that no crop variety is ever lost for good.

The need for such a facility is not obvious at first glance. Most of the food eaten around the world today comes from a surprisingly narrow band of crop varieties, even though a vast reservoir of genetic diversity survives in older and wild relatives of those same crops. That diversity, however, is mostly held in ordinary national and regional gene banks, of which there are well over a thousand scattered across the globe, and many of them are far from secure. A civil war, a natural disaster, or something as unglamorous as an unpaid electricity bill and a failing freezer can destroy decades of painstaking collecting work in a single stroke, wiping out varieties as completely, and as irreversibly, as the extinction of a species.

The Seed Vault was conceived as an insurance policy against precisely this kind of loss. Construction began in 2006, and the facility opened in February 2008, funded and run in partnership by the Norwegian government, the Nordic Genetic Resource Centre and the Crop Trust, an international organisation devoted to safeguarding crop diversity. Svalbard was chosen with care: it is politically stable and remote enough to be shielded from most conceivable disasters, yet still reachable by scheduled flight; the site sits comfortably above any plausible future sea level; and the surrounding rock is permanently frozen, providing a natural, low-cost backup to the vault's mechanical cooling system should that system ever fail.

Depositing seeds in the vault does not mean handing them over. Each contributing gene bank signs an agreement with the Norwegian government but retains full ownership of, and sole access to, its own seeds, which are sealed by the depositor in air-tight foil packages of around 500 seeds before being boxed and shipped north. Once inside the mountain, the boxes are stacked in chambers cooled to a constant −18°C, a temperature at which well-dried seeds of most species can, in theory, remain viable for centuries, and one that is reinforced, rather than replaced, by the surrounding permafrost.

The vault has room for around four and a half million distinct seed varieties, and in less than two decades it has come to hold well over a million samples, representing thousands of species and contributions from more than a hundred countries and institutions. Grains such as rice and wheat make up the bulk of the collection, but it also contains countless varieties of vegetables, fruit and forage crops, many of which are barely grown commercially anywhere today but which may carry genes for drought or disease resistance that plant breeders will need in future.

For its first seven years, the vault only ever received deposits. That changed in September 2015, when the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas, known as ICARDA, made the first withdrawal in the vault's history. ICARDA's own gene bank, based near Aleppo, had held one of the most important collections of wheat, barley, lentil and chickpea varieties from the Fertile Crescent, the region where these crops were first domesticated, but the escalating civil war in Syria made it impossible to keep the collection running safely. Because ICARDA had already duplicated more than 80% of its holdings in Svalbard before the fighting worsened, its scientists were able to retrieve tens of thousands of seed samples and use them to rebuild the collection from scratch at new sites in Lebanon and Morocco. Further withdrawals followed in 2017 and 2019, and ICARDA has since been steadily returning newly multiplied seed to Svalbard, restoring the very duplicate collection it once had to draw on.

The vault's design has not gone entirely untested. In 2016 and 2017, unusually warm weather combined with heavy rain to send meltwater seeping into the entrance tunnel; engineers responded quickly, and no seeds were harmed, but the incident prompted the Norwegian government to waterproof the tunnel walls and remove heat-generating equipment from the entrance area. It was a reminder that the very climate instability the vault exists to help humanity survive is itself capable of reaching, if not yet threatening, the vault itself.

None of this makes Svalbard a solution on its own. The vault stores seed, but it does not test it, grow it out, or breed with it; that ongoing work remains the job of the depositing gene banks, many of which still lack secure long-term funding. What Svalbard offers is something narrower but essential: a last line of defence, sitting quietly under the Arctic ice, for the moment when everything else has failed.

passages.title: Passage 2
passages.instructions:
Questions 14–26

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on the reading passage below.
passages.body:
Fifty years of one thousand lives: New Zealand's Dunedin Study

Most psychological and medical research relies on a brief snapshot of people's lives: a survey completed once, a scan taken on a single afternoon, an interview that lasts an hour. A very different kind of project has been quietly running in a small city on the South Island of New Zealand for more than half a century, following the same group of people from infancy into middle age. It is known simply as the Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study, and it has become one of the most closely watched research projects of its kind anywhere in the world.

The study began in the early 1970s, when researchers set out to follow every baby born at Dunedin's Queen Mary Maternity Hospital between April 1972 and March 1973. Roughly 91% of eligible families agreed to take part, giving the project a foundation cohort of 1,037 individuals. From the age of three, these children were brought back for testing every two years throughout childhood, and less frequently, but just as thoroughly, in adulthood, with major assessments at 18, 21, 26, 32, 38 and, most recently, 45. A further round, when members turn 52, is already being planned.

What sets the study apart from comparable projects elsewhere is not just its length but its extraordinarily high participation rate. At the most recent assessment, 94% of all surviving members took part, a figure researchers believe is unmatched by any study of similar design and duration anywhere in the world. Many long-running studies lose a large share of their original participants over the decades, and those who drop out are rarely a random cross-section of the group, which can quietly distort the findings. The Dunedin team has instead gone to considerable lengths to keep almost everyone involved, tracking members who have moved abroad and flying many of them back to New Zealand, at the study's expense, for each new round of testing.

The study is also unusual in how many different fields of research it draws on at once. Rather than focusing narrowly on one topic, it has gathered data on cardiovascular health, dental health, respiratory function, genetics and brain imaging, alongside detailed psychological and behavioural assessments, all on the same group of people across their entire lives. This multidisciplinary approach has generated well over a thousand peer-reviewed publications to date.

Among its best-known findings is one concerning self-control in early childhood. Researchers scored each child's ability to persist with a task, control impulses and delay gratification, based on assessments carried out by parents, teachers and independent observers at several points during childhood. Decades later, those who had scored lowest on self-control as children were, on average, more likely by their mid-forties to be in poorer physical health, to be struggling financially and to have a criminal conviction, even once differences in childhood intelligence and family background were taken into account. The finding has since influenced early-childhood policy in several countries.

A second widely cited result concerns mental health. By the age of 45, 86% of cohort members had experienced at least one diagnosable mental health condition at some point in their lives. Rather than being confined to a small, separate section of the population, episodes of mental illness turn out, on this evidence, to be close to a near-universal feature of the human life course, a conclusion that has fed into public debate about how mental health services ought to be organised and funded.

A third strand of research has focused on ageing itself. By repeatedly measuring biomarkers linked to the cardiovascular, metabolic, kidney, immune and respiratory systems between the ages of 26 and 45, researchers have been able to calculate each member's individual pace of biological ageing. People of exactly the same chronological age, it turns out, can be biologically ageing at markedly different speeds, and a faster pace of ageing in midlife has been linked to poorer outcomes in later life, including cognitive decline, well before any obvious illness appears.

None of this comes cheaply. Keeping a single cohort under such close observation for more than fifty years requires sustained funding, drawn in this case from the New Zealand government, the University of Otago, and international bodies including the United States' National Institutes of Health and the UK's Medical Research Council. It also requires enormous logistical effort simply to keep the study's members involved. But for the researchers who run it, that cost has bought something no shorter study could offer: a genuinely complete picture of how a single generation's health and circumstances unfold, one life at a time, from birth to middle age and beyond.

question_groups.title: Questions 14–19
question_groups.instructions:
Complete the summary using the list of words, A–J, below.

Write the correct letter, A–J, for each answer.

questions.question: Whereas most research offers only a ____ of people's lives, the Dunedin Study has followed the same individuals for decades.
The project has tracked its participants from birth all the way into ____.
The original cohort was recruited in the early 1970s, achieving a remarkably high rate of ____ among eligible families.
Even after several decades, the study has managed to maintain an unusually ____ follow-up rate compared with similar projects elsewhere.
Because it combines so many different academic fields, the study is often described as genuinely ____ in nature.
Its findings have so far appeared in more than a thousand ____ articles.
The Dunedin Study has found a connection between children's self-control and their circumstances later in life.
Most cohort members first experienced a mental health condition before the age of 18.
People of the same chronological age can differ in how fast they are ageing biologically, according to the study.
Every member of the original 1,037-person cohort has taken part in every single round of testing since 1972.
What does the passage suggest is unusual about the Dunedin Study's rate of participation?
answer_options: It is the first study ever to follow people from birth into old age.
It has a higher follow-up rate than other studies of comparable length and design.
It only recruited families who had already agreed never to leave New Zealand.
It depends mainly on payment to keep members involved.
questions.correct_answer: It has a higher follow-up rate than other studies of comparable length and design.

questions.question: What does the study's finding about mental health conditions challenge?
answer_options: The idea that mental illness typically develops in early childhood.
The assumption that biological ageing cannot be measured before old age.
The view that mental health difficulties affect only a small, distinct section of the population.
The belief that childhood self-control has no effect on adult wellbeing.
questions.correct_answer: The view that mental health difficulties affect only a small, distinct section of the population.

questions.question: Why, according to the passage, has running the Dunedin Study been so demanding?
answer_options: Because members must be flown back to New Zealand for testing wherever they now live.
Because most of its funding comes from private commercial sponsors.
Because each participant is tested on a daily basis.
Because entirely new participants must be recruited at every stage.
questions.correct_answer: Because members must be flown back to New Zealand for testing wherever they now live.

passages.title: Passage 3
passages.instructions:
Questions 27–40

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on the reading passage below.
passages.body:
Cremona: how a five-hundred-year-old craft came back from the brink

In a city of only around 70,000 people in northern Italy, more than 150 workshops still turn out violins, violas and cellos entirely by hand, using methods that have barely changed since the sixteenth century. Cremona's reputation as the spiritual home of the violin rests above all on three family names still spoken of, among musicians and instrument-makers, with something close to reverence: Amati, Guarneri and Stradivari.

Andrea Amati is generally credited with establishing the basic form of the modern violin in Cremona in the mid-1500s, and his descendants, in particular his grandson Nicolò Amati, went on to train a generation of makers who would eventually eclipse even their teacher. Among Nicolò's pupils was a young man named Antonio Stradivari, who inherited more than a century of accumulated local expertise and, over a working life that ran from the 1660s until his death in 1737, refined it into instruments still regarded by many as the finest ever made. His near-contemporary Giuseppe Guarneri, known as 'del Gesù', produced violins prized by generations of soloists for their darker, more powerful tone, and debate over the relative merits of the two workshops' output has never entirely been settled.

That golden era did not last. Quality and reputation slid from the end of the eighteenth century onwards, and by the early twentieth century Cremona had lost not only many of its makers but much of its accumulated technical knowledge: workshops closed, family businesses ended, and a number of the city's remaining luthiers left for places offering better prospects. For a time, it looked entirely possible that the tradition responsible for the world's most celebrated stringed instruments might simply die out in the city that had given birth to it.

The turning point came in the years following the bicentenary of Stradivari's death in 1937, when a dedicated school of violin-making was established in Cremona with the explicit aim of recovering craftsmanship that had nearly been lost over the previous century. Because there was no unbroken chain of instruction left to draw on, its early teachers had to reconstruct many techniques largely from surviving instruments and archival fragments. Among the figures most closely associated with this rebuilding effort was Francesco Bissolotti, who taught at the school for more than twenty years while also running a workshop of his own, where he trained not only outside students but his own four sons in the craft; alongside contemporaries such as Gio Batta Morassi, he is widely credited with having played a decisive part in the city's recovery.

Since the middle of the twentieth century, Cremonese violin-making has been undergoing a steady renaissance, drawing apprentices from around the world who now train, and often go on to settle, in the city. In 2012, the craft was added to UNESCO's list of humanity's Intangible Cultural Heritage, and every three years Cremona hosts an international competition in which entrants from across the globe have their instruments judged against the standards set by the historic workshops. The methods on display, however, look remarkably close to those Stradivari himself would have recognised: makers still choose maple for the back, ribs and neck of an instrument and spruce for its front, still shape almost every part of the instrument by hand rather than by machine, and still apply layers of varnish whose precise historical recipes, in Stradivari's case at least, continue to be investigated by scientists to this day.

What the revival has not been able to shortcut is time. A single violin, made in the traditional manner, can take a skilled luthier many weeks of work from start to finish, and the underlying skills, from judging properly seasoned wood to sensing the correct thickness of an unfinished front plate by touch and by ear, are still passed on chiefly through years of hands-on apprenticeship in a workshop rather than through formal instruction alone. It is this combination of a formal school and a living apprenticeship tradition that has allowed knowledge nearly extinguished a century ago to be handed on to a new generation of makers, leaving a craft that once seemed destined to disappear looking, for now at least, reasonably secure.

question_groups.title: Questions 27–32
question_groups.instructions:
Complete the summary using the list of words, A–J, below.

Write the correct letter, A–J, for each answer.

questions.question: Despite having fewer than 100,000 inhabitants, Cremona is still home to well over a hundred workshops making instruments entirely by ____.
The city's reputation rests on three family names regarded by many as ____ in the history of the violin.
Andrea Amati is credited with giving the violin its ____ form in the mid-1500s.
His descendants went on to train a number of highly ____ makers, including Antonio Stradivari.
The ____ that Stradivari and his contemporaries reached could not be maintained indefinitely.
Quality and reputation began to ____ from the end of the eighteenth century onwards.
The violin-making school set up in Cremona in the twentieth century continued an unbroken tradition of instruction handed down from Stradivari's own workshop.
Francesco Bissolotti taught only at the violin-making school and did not run a workshop of his own.
Cremona's tradition of violin-making has been recognised by UNESCO.
Most of Cremona's current luthiers trained personally under Francesco Bissolotti.
What point does the writer make about the methods used by today's Cremonese makers?
answer_options: They rely heavily on machinery to speed up production.
They closely resemble the techniques used centuries earlier.
They differ considerably from one workshop to another.
They no longer involve the use of traditional varnishes.
questions.correct_answer: They closely resemble the techniques used centuries earlier.

questions.question: According to the passage, what remains true of Stradivari's varnish?
answer_options: Its exact recipe has now been fully identified.
It has been replaced by more durable modern alternatives.
Its precise composition is still being investigated by researchers.
It was never considered important to an instrument's tone.
questions.correct_answer: Its precise composition is still being investigated by researchers.

questions.question: What does the writer suggest about how violin-making skills are passed on today?
answer_options: Mainly through formal courses rather than hands-on practice.
Chiefly through years of practical apprenticeship in a workshop.
Largely without the need for any traditional training.
More quickly now than in Stradivari's time.
questions.correct_answer: Chiefly through years of practical apprenticeship in a workshop.

questions.question: What overall impression does the passage give of Cremona's violin-making tradition today?
answer_options: It is likely to disappear again within a generation.
It survives mainly as a tourist attraction rather than genuine craft.
It has recovered sufficiently to look secure for now.
It is now regarded less highly abroad than it was in Stradivari's era.
questions.correct_answer: It has recovered sufficiently to look secure for now.
